opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to the nature of the signal itself. I've always loved working on visual data. Images and video are so rich, and there's something very satisfying about generating a picture or a scene and seeing it come alive. But when I thought seriously about where intelligence would show up first, language seemed like the obvious candidate.

Language is already a compressed representation of human knowledge. When people write, they've done a huge amount of abstraction for you. The concepts, the reasoning, the relationships between things are all encoded in a fairly compact form. So when you train a model to predict the next word, you're essentially training it to absorb how humans think and organize the world. The signal-to-noise ratio is very high.

Visual signals are very different. A video has an enormous number of pixels, and most of them are redundant or irrelevant to what you actually care about. The model has to figure out on its own what matters: objects, physics, cause and effect. Nobody has abstracted it for you. That makes it much harder to learn intelligence directly from pixels, and it needs far more data and compute to get to the same level of understanding.

There's also the data question. The internet gave us a huge amount of text, and it's relatively cheap to process. Video is plentiful too, but it's much more expensive to train on, and it's harder to get the right supervision out of it.

So my expectation was that language would get there first, and that has largely played out. But I don't think that makes vision less important. If we want AI that can act in the physical world, like robots or autonomous vehicles, the model has to understand space, motion, and physics, and you can't fully get that from text. That's why I've stayed excited about visual generation and world models. I think language opened the door, and the next big step is grounding that intelligence in the physical world through visual signals.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts abstracted language with pixel-heavy visual signals, but does not characterize visual signals as observations of the world rather than the essence of knowledge.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a compact, abstract representation encoding concepts and reasoning, while visual signals require learning from pixels. This communicates why language is closer to symbolic representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the nature of the signal itself. Language is a human-made abstraction. We invented it specifically to compress the world and to describe it efficiently. So a lot of the hard work of turning raw observations into concepts has already been done by humans before the data even reaches the model. The text on the internet is essentially the output of billions of people reasoning about the world and writing down the conclusions. If you train a model on that, you're training it on a very dense, pre-distilled form of intelligence.

Visual signals are the opposite. A video is just pixels. There's no labeling of which object matters, no built-in notion of cause and effect, no explicit structure. The information is extremely redundant. You could have a thousand frames and most of them are nearly identical. So the model has to discover the abstractions itself, from scratch, which is a much harder learning problem. And you need orders of magnitude more compute to extract the same amount of understanding.

So even though I've always been drawn to vision, because that's how biological intelligence actually developed, I thought it was pretty clear that language would get there first. Language was the shortcut. The abstractions were handed to the model for free. With vision, you have to earn them, and that takes a lot longer and a lot more data.

But I'd also say that I think the order doesn't change the final destination. Eventually, if you want a system that can act in the physical world, it has to understand the physical world directly, not just through descriptions humans wrote about it. Language models know what the word "gravity" means. A world model has to know what gravity does. So language first, but not language only.

r001.rationale: The response describes video as pixels and raw observations that lack explicit structure, while language contains human-created abstractions and conclusions about the world.

r002.rationale: It attributes language’s head start to text being a compressed, abstract, pre-distilled representation of ideas, unlike visual signals, which require the model to discover abstractions.

astra-6.text:
I preferred working on visual signals, but I thought language was a more direct route to intelligence. Language is how we express concepts, explain relationships, and communicate our reasoning. So when you learn from language, you’re learning from information that people have already organized into something meaningful.

With visual signals, you have to discover that structure from the raw observations. An image contains a lot of information, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what matters or why something happened. That’s what made vision interesting to me, but it also made me expect that we would see intelligence emerge in language first.

r001.rationale: The response describes visual input as raw observations whose structure must be discovered, but does not distinguish observations of the world from the essence of knowledge.

r002.rationale: It says language conveys organized meaning and reasoning, but does not attribute the expectation to language being closer to symbolic representations than vision.

sol-6.1.text: I preferred working on visual signals because they felt very concrete—you could look at an image and see what the system was getting right or wrong. But I thought language was a more likely place for intelligence to emerge first because so much human knowledge is already expressed in text. Language carries facts, concepts, and the ways people reason about the world. To model it really well, a system has to learn something beyond the surface patterns of words. So my personal interest was in vision, but my intuition was that language offered a more direct path to broad intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes images as concrete and visually inspectable, but does not distinguish visual signals as observations of the world from the essence of knowledge.

r002.rationale: It says text expresses knowledge and language may offer a direct path to intelligence, but does not explain this in terms of language being closer to symbolic representations than visual signals.
